prose_changes.old: The Christians of the Malabar coast traced their church to the apostle Thomas and had for centuries received their bishops from the Church of the East, worshipping in Syriac. The Portuguese found this puzzling and then intolerable, and in 1599 Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes convened a synod at Diamper that placed the community under Latin jurisdiction, revised its liturgy, and ordered its Syriac books corrected or burned. Half a century of resentment came to a head on 3 January 1653, when a crowd gathered at a stone cross in Mattancherry, tied ropes to it and swore they would no longer obey the Jesuits. The Coonan Cross Oath, so called because the cross was said to have bent under the strain.
prose_changes.new: The Christians of the Malabar coast traced their church to the apostle Thomas. For centuries they had worshipped in Syriac and taken their bishops from the Church of the East. The Portuguese found this puzzling and then intolerable. In 1599 Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes held a synod at Diamper. It placed the community under Latin rule, revised its liturgy, and ordered its Syriac books corrected or burned. Half a century of resentment came to a head on 3 January 1653. At Mattancherry a crowd swore they would no longer obey the Jesuits or the Jesuit archbishop, Francisco Garcia. Tradition says they tied ropes to a stone cross as they swore. This is the Coonan Cross Oath, named for a cross said to have bent under the strain.
prose_changes.reason: The oath sentence stated the rope-and-stone-cross scene as fact. Sebastiani (1666, lines 663-666) puts the oath in the church before a crucifix and names Archbishop Garcia; the 1787 community document says only that they assembled at Mattancherry. The scene is now marked as tradition, Garcia is named, and the final fragment ('The Coonan Cross Oath, so called...') is made a sentence. The first two sentences were split to bring the field to the readability floor; substance unchanged.

prose_changes.old: Ahmad Gragn's jihad devastates the church (1529-43); Wayna Daga (1543) saves it; the Jesuit interlude ends in Susenyos's Catholicism (1622), popular revolt, and Fasilides's restoration and expulsion of the Jesuits (1632) - the era's inversion: the Counter-Reformation as outside pressure on an ancient church
prose_changes.new: Ahmad Gragn's jihad lays waste to the church from 1529 to 1543, until the battle of Wayna Daga saves it. Then the Jesuits come. Emperor Susenyos turns Catholic in 1622, his people revolt, and the old faith comes back in 1632. His son Fasilides drives out the Jesuits in 1634. It is the era turned upside down: here the Counter-Reformation is the outside force pressing on an old church.
prose_changes.reason: The old text dated the expulsion of the Jesuits to 1632; Lobo (lines 1667-1669) gives 1634, and Telles has the old faith restored by proclamation first. Whole field rewritten from note form into sentences to pass the readability floor; every event and the 'inversion' reading are kept.

prose_changes.old: Opponents of hereditary succession elect Yohannan Sulaqa; he professes at Rome (1553), is consecrated in St Peter's, and is martyred (1555) - the Chaldean line begins and the communion carries two rival patriarchates ever after; kin story: the Coonan Cross Oath in Malabar is the same communion's other seventeenth-century ordeal. Told within the Church of the East, Timur to Hakkari, with the Chaldean consolidation as the continuation.
prose_changes.new: Opponents of the hereditary succession elect Yohannan Sulaqa. Rome makes him patriarch in 1553, and he is killed at home in 1555. From then on the communion has two rival patriarchs. In Malabar, the same communion's Indian church faced its own crisis under Portuguese rule, which ended in the Coonan Cross Oath of 1653. The story grows out of the Church of the East of Timur's age and the Hakkari mountains. The Chaldean consolidation of the 1800s carries it on.
prose_changes.reason: Four fixes. 'Consecrated in St Peter's': no cited source names the church. 'The Chaldean line begins' contradicts the legacy field and the sources' dispute over which line became Chaldean. 'The same communion's other seventeenth-century ordeal' makes the 1552 schism seventeenth-century. 'Told within ... with ... as the continuation' was cataloguing language; it now states the relationships. 'Martyred' (the Roman sources' word) is made neutral: Badger and Wigram report other accounts of his death. Whole field rewritten for the readability floor.

prose_changes.old: The division is still the shape of the communion, though not in the way the 1552 parties would have guessed. The line Sulaqa began eventually drifted back out of communion with Rome and continued as the Assyrian Church of the East, now largely a diaspora church with its patriarchate at Erbil, while the older line he had challenged entered communion with Rome in the nineteenth century and became the Chaldean Catholic Church, today the largest Christian body in Iraq. Both still use the East Syriac liturgy, including the ancient Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the two churches have been in formal dialogue since the 1990s.
prose_changes.new: The division is still the shape of the communion, though not in the way the 1552 parties would have guessed. Two churches came out of it, and their histories disagree about which line is which. A Catholic list of patriarchs from 1877 has Sulaqa's line drift back out of communion with Rome. On that reading it continued as the Assyrian Church of the East, now largely a diaspora church with its patriarchate at Erbil. The older line he had challenged entered communion with Rome in the nineteenth century. It became the Chaldean Catholic Church, today the largest Christian body in Iraq. But in the 1840s the mountain church itself traced its patriarchs to Sulaqa's rival. Both still use the East Syriac liturgy, including the ancient Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The two churches have been in formal dialogue since the 1990s.
prose_changes.reason: The text stated as settled which line became which church. The cited sources disagree: Lamy (1877, series III, through Simeon XV at Qudshanis) runs Sulaqa's line to the mountain patriarchs; Badger (1852, lines 7897-7903) reports the mountain church's own claim to descend from Sulaqa's rival, and Wigram (1929, lines 7438-7461) puts Sulaqa's line on the plain. The reading is kept, attributed, and the other account named. Long sentences split for the readability floor.
